newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian government urges central bank to cut rates.
newsitem.headline: Indian government urges central bank to cut rates.

text.p: India's government, keen to ensure continued robust economic growth, urged the central bank on Monday to cut interest rates and spur bank lending.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor C. Rangarajan that the annual inflation rate should be kept at six to seven percent to provide economic and political stability, the RBI said in a statement.

"Finance Minister also urged that while there has been some softening of interest rates since October 1996, it is not enough and further reduction of lending rates would be desirable and possible," the RBI statement said.

Chidambaram told Reuters at the weekend that interest rates, adjusted for inflation, had fallen to between eight and nine percent from 17-18 percent last June when Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government assumed power.
But he said rates could be cut further and urged the central bank chief to encourage bankers to lend more actively as credit had expanded slowly.
"Some banks are willing to lend, others are not," the statement quoted Chidambaram as saying. "Such slow growth of credit is simply unacceptable."
Bank credit increased by 152 billion rupees ($4.2 billion) from April 1996 to January 1997, only half as much as in the same 10-month period in 1995/96, according to government figures.
"Measures necessary to accelerate the flow of credit to support growth in output will merit attention," the RBI chief said.

Last month Chidambaram presented a budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) fiscal year that would slash corporate and personal income taxes. The budget is based on the premise that continued strong economic growth will help boost tax revenues and reduce pervasive poverty.
Gross domestic product (GDP) will rise by an estimated 6.8 percent in the current 1996/97 fiscal year. The government aims for at least 7.0 percent growth in the next financial year.

The RBI quoted Chidambaram as telling the RBI governor that price stability is critical since it is a key to maintaining growth and "inflation should be contained at 6-7 percent as this would provide both economic and poltical stability".
The annual inflation rate as measured by the wholesale price index was 7.78 percent in the week ended on March 1, up from 5.13 percent one year earlier.

Chidambaram said the past fiscal year had been "difficult" for prices because of a drop in wheat production and an increase in the prices of state-controlled goods such as oil, which had been held steady ahead of elections in April/May of 1996.
The government is considering another rise in domestic oil prices, which analysts say could spur inflation.
The finance minister said the interest tax on banks had been reduced, and suggested that the cost of banks' transactions needed to be cut to help ease lending rates.

The RBI governor said the central bank's monetary policy would continue to be two-fold -- regulating the money supply to keep inflationary pressures under control and providing adequate credit to support growth.
He said large inflows of foreign capital, drawn to Indian stock markets and into industrial projects, would complicate its task of keeping money supply growth at the target level of 16 percent.
